def: A 6-byte packet (plus 2 bytes of framing) exchanged between the Data Link Layers of the two ports on one PCIe link, carrying Ack/Nak, flow-control credits, power-management handshakes or vendor data. Never forwarded through switches and never seen by software.
The middle PCIe layer: makes one link reliable with sequence numbers, LCRC and Ack/Nak replay, and runs flow-control initialisation and credit updates.
A 12-bit number (0–4095, wrapping) the Data Link Layer attaches to every TLP in non-flit mode so the receiver can detect lost or duplicated TLPs and acknowledge them cumulatively.
32-bit CRC appended by the Data Link Layer to each TLP (non-flit mode), covering the sequence number and the TLP; checked and regenerated at every hop.
Transmitter memory holding every sent TLP until an Ack or Nak covers it, so it can be retransmitted unchanged after a Nak or replay timer expiry.
Transmitter timer that triggers a replay of all unacknowledged TLPs if no forward-progress Ack/Nak arrives in time; expiry is logged as the correctable error Replay Timer Timeout.
2-bit counter of consecutive replays without forward progress; when it rolls over the Data Link Layer directs the Physical Layer to retrain the link and logs REPLAY_NUM Rollover (correctable).
Ack (type 00h) acknowledges every TLP up to its sequence number; Nak (type 10h) acknowledges up to its sequence number and requests replay of everything after it.
A TLP deliberately cancelled by its transmitter mid-transmission (inverted LCRC and end-bad framing), typically by a cut-through switch; the receiver discards it silently and logs no error.
The Data Link Control and Management State Machine state in which TLPs may flow; reached from DL_Inactive through DL_Init (FC_INIT1, FC_INIT2) after flow-control initialisation.

PCIe 6.0+ mode in which TLPs and DLLPs are packed into fixed 256-byte flits protected by flit CRC and FEC, with retry per flit instead of per-TLP sequence numbers and LCRC. Mandatory at 64.0 GT/s and above.
A Physical-Layer-only component that recovers and re-transmits the signal on a long channel; it does not acknowledge TLPs or hold credits, unlike a switch.
PCIe mechanism by which a receiver advertises buffer space (credits) per traffic category so the transmitter never sends a TLP the receiver cannot accept. Per link, per Virtual Channel.
Unit of receiver buffer space: one header credit per TLP header, one data credit per 16 bytes (4 DW). Six types: PH, PD, NPH, NPD, CplH, CplD.

term: PH / PD / NPH / NPD / CplH / CplD
exp: Posted, Non-Posted and Completion Header/Data credits
def: The six PCIe flow-control credit types; e.g. a 256-byte MWr consumes 1 PH + 16 PD, an MRd 1 NPH, a 64-byte CplD 1 CplH + 4 CplD.
An initial flow-control advertisement of 0 for a header or data field, meaning the receiver will always accept that type; Endpoints advertise infinite completion credits.
DLLP by which a receiver returns credits as its buffers drain; carries the running total of credits allocated, so a lost UpdateFC is corrected by the next one.
DLLPs exchanged after link-up to advertise initial Posted, Non-Posted and Completion credits for a Virtual Channel (InitFC1), then confirm receipt (InitFC2).
PCIe 4.0+ extension that scales the header and data credit fields (HdrScale/DataScale) so a receiver can advertise more credits for high-speed, high-latency links.
The propagation of a slow receiver's lack of credits back toward the sender, hop by hop: transmitters wait, no error is logged.
The configuration address of a PCI function: 8-bit bus, 5-bit device, 3-bit function, e.g. 01:00.0; as a 16-bit value it is the Requester/Completer ID.
Memory-mapped window giving each function's 4 KiB configuration space an address: base + (bus<<20) + (device<<15) + (function<<12) + offset.
Completion status a function returns to a configuration request while it is not yet ready after reset; with CRS Software Visibility, a Vendor ID read returns 0001h.
The 4 KiB per-function register space (256 bytes in conventional PCI) holding identification, capabilities, control and error status; accessed with configuration requests.
Non-posted TLPs that read or write configuration space; Type 0 targets the bus below the issuing port, Type 1 is forwarded by bridges.
Type 1 header registers (18h/19h/1Ah) holding a bridge's own bus, the bus directly below it, and the highest bus number below it; used to route configuration requests.
Optional capability that treats the 8 device+function bits as a single function number, allowing up to 256 functions in one device (important for SR-IOV).
The 64-byte configuration header layout of Endpoints (Vendor/Device ID, Command/Status, Class Code, six BARs, Subsystem IDs, Capabilities Pointer, interrupt fields).
The configuration header layout of bridges (Root Ports, switch ports): two BARs, bus number registers and I/O, memory and prefetchable memory windows.
Later-PCIe mechanisms (Device Readiness Status, Function Readiness Status, Immediate Readiness) that let a function tell software it is ready sooner than the default post-reset wait.
Linked list of capability structures in configuration space 40h–FFh, starting at the Capabilities Pointer (34h); each entry has an ID byte and a next-pointer byte.
Capability structure in configuration space 100h–FFFh with a 16-bit ID, 4-bit version and 12-bit next offset; the list starts at 100h (e.g. AER 0001h, SR-IOV 0010h).
Three bytes at 09h–0Bh (programming interface, sub-class, base class) giving a function's generic type; NVMe is 01h/08h/02h.
Interrupt mechanism using a table (in a BAR) of independent address/data/mask entries; each interrupt is a posted Memory Write. Configured through capability ID 11h.
Extended capability (0010h) letting a Physical Function expose Virtual Functions with their own Routing IDs and VF BARs.
PCIe extended capability (ID 0001h) with detailed uncorrectable and correctable error status, mask and severity registers, plus a header log of the offending TLP.
Configuration register describing a device memory or I/O region (type, 32/64-bit, prefetchable, size via hard-wired zero bits) and holding the base address software assigns.
A memory region whose reads have no side effects and whose writes may be merged; can be mapped write-combining and placed in a bridge's 64-bit prefetchable window.
Base/Limit register pairs in a Type 1 header that define which I/O, non-prefetchable (32-bit) and prefetchable (64-bit capable) memory addresses a bridge forwards downstream.
Optional extended capability letting software choose among several sizes for a BAR before assigning it.
Placement of a BAR region at an address that is a multiple of its (power-of-two) size, a consequence of the hard-wired zero low-order bits.
Access to device registers or memory through ordinary CPU loads and stores to addresses inside a BAR; stores become posted MWr TLPs, loads become MRd with a completion.
Write-only NVMe register in BAR0 (from 1000h, stride 4 << CAP.DSTRD) that the host writes with a new SQ tail or CQ head.
Data movement performed by a device's own engines issuing memory reads and writes to host memory, without the CPU copying the data.
Data movement in which the CPU itself reads and writes device registers for every word — slow and CPU-intensive compared with DMA.
Configuration Command register bit that allows a function to issue memory and I/O requests (DMA, MSI/MSI-X); on bridges it controls forwarding of upstream requests.
The address a device places in its DMA requests (dma_addr_t in Linux); translated to a physical address by the IOMMU, or identical to it without translation.
Root Complex unit that translates device-issued IOVAs to physical addresses per Requester ID, enforces permissions, and logs faults (e.g. Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, Arm SMMU).
Cache of IOMMU translations; misses require page-table walks that add DMA latency.
Linux mechanism that copies DMA data through buffers the device can reach when it cannot reach the original memory directly; correct but costs CPU copies.
Attribute telling the Root Complex that a DMA access need not be snooped against CPU caches; safe only when software guarantees coherence.
Optional PCIe capability letting a device request and cache address translations from the IOMMU.
List of (address, length) segments describing one logical buffer spread over non-contiguous memory; NVMe PRP lists and SGLs are scatter-gather structures.
Linux DMA allocation of long-lived memory that CPU and device may access concurrently without explicit sync calls; used for NVMe queues.
Linux mapping of existing memory for a transfer; ownership passes to the device until unmap or sync, with cache maintenance done at those points.
